clinicalPearls: Caused by the obligate intracellular parasite Toxoplasma gondii; up to a third of the world's population is latently infected (Harrison 22e p.1797).

Two transmissible stages reach humans: tissue cysts containing bradyzoites in undercooked meat (e.g., lamb, pork, venison, ground beef), and sporulated oocysts shed in cat feces that contaminate soil, food, or water; sporulated oocysts are environmentally hardy and highly infectious (Harrison 22e p.1797).
In the immunocompetent host, acute infection is usually asymptomatic and self-limited, going unrecognized in 80-90% of acquired infections (Harrison 22e p.1799).

The most common manifestation of symptomatic acute toxoplasmosis in immunocompetent patients is cervical lymphadenopathy; nodes are usually nontender and discrete, with associated headache, malaise, fatigue, and low-grade fever (temperature usually <40 degrees C) (Harrison 22e p.1799).

The classic severe presentation is reactivation encephalitis in immunocompromised hosts (especially HIV-positive individuals or transplant recipients) in whom latent infection has reactivated (Harrison 22e p.1797).

In AIDS, >95% of Toxoplasma encephalitis cases are due to recrudescent infection, typically developing when the CD4+ T-cell count falls below 100/microL; encephalitis is the predominant manifestation while meningeal involvement is uncommon (Harrison 22e p.1800).

On MRI/CT, Toxoplasma encephalitis classically produces multiple ring-enhancing lesions, most often in the basal ganglia and corticomedullary junction; a single lesion increases the likelihood of primary CNS lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.1801-1802).

T. gondii is the most common cause of posterior uveitis in immunocompetent individuals and is estimated to cause about 35% of all chorioretinitis cases in the US and Europe (Harrison 22e p.1799, p.1801).

Congenital toxoplasmosis results from transplacental passage during primary maternal infection; infants may be asymptomatic at birth but later manifest chorioretinitis, strabismus, epilepsy, hydrocephalus, microcephaly, intellectual disability, and psychomotor retardation (Harrison 22e p.1797, p.1799).

Antibody titers are NOT useful for establishing reactivation or following infection activity in immunocompromised patients; however, an absence of positive serology suggests an alternative diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1800).
Diagnosis rests on serology (combined IgG and IgM, with circulating IgA favoring acute infection) and PCR; PCR of body fluids is specific but its sensitivity may be low (Harrison 22e p.1801).

A therapeutic trial of anti-Toxoplasma medications is frequently used in AIDS patients with CNS mass lesions: >50% improve by day 3 and >90% by day 7, whereas worsening by day 7 (or lymphoma) prompts brain biopsy (Harrison 22e p.1802).
harrison.pathophysiology: T. gondii is an intracellular coccidian. Ingested tissue cysts (bradyzoites) or oocysts (sporozoites) release organisms that invade gut epithelium and transform into rapidly dividing tachyzoites, which can infect and replicate in all nucleated mammalian cells via a parasitophorous vacuole, causing cell death and focal necrosis with an acute mononuclear inflammatory response. Parasites disseminate as free tachyzoites or within phagocytic 'Trojan horse' cells through blood and lymphatics to lymphatic tissue, skeletal muscle, myocardium, retina, placenta, and CNS. In the immunocompetent host, humoral and cell-mediated immunity (parasiticidal antibody, macrophage activation, IFN-gamma, IL-12-driven TH1 response, CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes) controls infection; tissue cysts containing bradyzoites then form 7-10 days after systemic infection and persist principally in the CNS and muscle, completing the asexual cycle and establishing lifelong chronic infection. Subclinical cycles of cyst rupture and reformation are the probable source of recrudescent infection. Immunocompromised or fetal hosts lack the immune factors (notably CD8+ T cells; reactivating T cells fail to secrete IFN-gamma and IL-2) needed to contain tachyzoite spread, allowing progressive focal destruction (necrotizing encephalitis, pneumonia, myocarditis). The sexual stage occurs only in the cat (definitive host), producing oocysts shed in feces (Harrison 22e p.1797-1800).
additionalDifferentials: Mononucleosis-like syndrome from acute toxoplasmic lymphadenopathy: EBV infection, CMV infection, HIV infection, Bartonella (cat-scratch disease), and lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.1800-1801).

CNS mass lesions in an AIDS patient: primary CNS lymphoma, metastatic tumor, brain abscess, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (JC virus), fungal infection, and mycobacterial infection (Harrison 22e p.1801).
Chorioretinitis in an immunocompetent individual: tuberculosis, syphilis, and histoplasmosis (Harrison 22e p.1801).
Chorioretinitis in an AIDS patient: CMV, syphilis, HSV, VZV, and fungal infection (Harrison 22e p.1801).
Cerebral toxoplasmosis must also be differentiated from herpes simplex encephalitis, cryptococcal meningitis, and HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND) (Harrison 22e p.1800).
Congenital infection: CMV, HSV, rubella, syphilis, and listeriosis (Harrison 22e p.1801).
infectionMimics: Primary CNS lymphoma (EBV-associated) presenting as ring-enhancing brain lesion(s) in AIDS
Tuberculous, fungal, or bacterial brain abscess
Pneumocystis pneumonia (Toxoplasma pneumonia can be confused with it)
nonInfectiousMimics: Metastatic brain tumor / other CNS malignancy
additionalInvestigations: Serology: combined IgG and IgM antibody to Toxoplasma; circulating IgA favors acute infection; Sabin-Feldman dye test, indirect fluorescent antibody test, and ELISA measure IgG; double-sandwich IgM-ELISA or IgM-ISAGA preferred for IgM (Harrison 22e p.1801).
IgG avidity testing to help time infection, particularly useful in pregnancy (Harrison 22e p.1801).

PCR amplification of T. gondii DNA from blood, CSF, ocular fluid, bronchoalveolar lavage, or amniotic fluid; PCR is the mainstay for detecting organisms but a negative PCR does not rule out toxoplasmosis (Harrison 22e p.1801).
Double-dose contrast CT and contrast MRI of the brain (standard imaging for Toxoplasma encephalitis); MRI is more sensitive for monitoring response (Harrison 22e p.1802).
CSF analysis in suspected CNS disease (modest pleocytosis and protein elevation without glucose change; CSF PCR specific but not sensitive) (Harrison 22e p.1800-1801).
Lymph node biopsy / histology showing follicular hyperplasia and clusters of epithelioid macrophages; demonstration of tachyzoites establishes acute infection (Harrison 22e p.1799, p.1801).
Dilated ophthalmologic examination for chorioretinitis; ocular fluid PCR, Western blot, or Goldmann-Witmer coefficient for ocular disease (Harrison 22e p.1801-1802).
In HIV-infected persons, screening for IgG antibody to Toxoplasma at the time of HIV diagnosis to identify latent infection (Harrison 22e p.1801).
Weekly blood PCR screening after allogeneic HSCT in patients seropositive before transplant; pre-transplant donor and recipient serologies (Harrison 22e p.1800).
Next-generation sequencing (metagenomics) of blood or body fluids, especially in immunocompromised individuals (Harrison 22e p.1801).
redFlags: Focal neurologic deficits, seizures, altered mental status, or ring-enhancing CNS mass lesion(s) in an HIV/AIDS patient (especially CD4+ <100/microL) - reactivation Toxoplasma encephalitis, which is rapidly fatal if untreated (Harrison 22e p.1800).
A solitary ring-enhancing CNS lesion - increases the likelihood of primary CNS lymphoma over toxoplasmosis (Harrison 22e p.1802).
Failure to improve clinically by day 7 of empiric anti-Toxoplasma therapy - prompts brain biopsy and consideration of lymphoma or alternative diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1802).
Fulminant sepsis, fever of unknown origin, or pneumonia in an immunocompetent person with travel to or residence in South/Central America - virulent atypical genotypes (Harrison 22e p.1797-1799).

Toxoplasma pneumonia / disseminated disease in immunocompromised hosts may progress to acute respiratory failure with hemoptysis, metabolic acidosis, hypotension, and disseminated intravascular coagulation (Harrison 22e p.1800).
Acute maternal infection in pregnancy (risk of transplacental transmission; severity highest with first-trimester infection) (Harrison 22e p.1798).
harrison.prognosis: In immunocompetent individuals, acute infection is usually asymptomatic and self-limited, resolving within several weeks though lymphadenopathy may persist for months; chronic infection persists lifelong with little consequence. Ocular disease can be self-limited but episodic chorioretinitis flares progressively destroy retinal tissue and may lead to glaucoma. In immunocompromised hosts, disease may be rapidly fatal if untreated, mandating prompt diagnosis and therapy; with treatment of Toxoplasma encephalitis, >50% improve by day 3 and >90% by day 7, but relapses are common and maintenance/secondary prophylaxis is needed while CD4+ counts remain low. For congenital toxoplasmosis, factors associated with severe disability include delayed diagnosis/treatment, neonatal hypoxia and hypoglycemia, profound visual impairment, uncorrected hydrocephalus, and raised intracranial pressure; with appropriate treatment upward of 70% of children have normal developmental, neurologic, and ophthalmologic findings at follow-up. Infected infants normal at birth may still have higher rates of learning disabilities and chronic neurologic sequelae (Harrison 22e p.1797-1801).
pitfalls: Acute toxoplasmosis is asymptomatic and self-limited in 80-90% of immunocompetent adults and children, so the diagnosis is easily missed (in one epidemic, toxoplasmosis was correctly diagnosed in only 3 of 25 patients who sought care) (Harrison 22e p.1799).
Antibody titers do not establish reactivation or track infection activity in immunocompromised patients; do not rely on serial titers to gauge active disease (Harrison 22e p.1800).
A negative PCR does not rule out toxoplasmosis - PCR is specific but may be of low sensitivity depending on the body fluid (Harrison 22e p.1801).

Isolation/demonstration of tissue cysts (bradyzoites) from biopsied tissue indicates only the presence of cysts and should NOT be misinterpreted as evidence of acute toxoplasmosis; only demonstration of tachyzoites (e.g., in lymph nodes) establishes acute infection (Harrison 22e p.1801).

IgM can persist for >1 year, so a positive IgM with positive IgG should not necessarily be interpreted as acute disease; a negative IgM with positive IgG indicates distant infection (Harrison 22e p.1801).
MRI/CT findings are not pathognomonic - 40% of CNS lymphomas are multifocal and 50% are ring-enhancing, and the false-negative rate for both MRI and CT is ~10% (Harrison 22e p.1802).

In AIDS patients with TE, IgM is usually undetectable and titers may be borderline/low (or transplant patients on B-cell-targeted immunosuppression may become seronegative); fewer than 3% have no demonstrable antibody at diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1800, p.1801).
Up to 25% of congenitally infected newborns may be seronegative with normal routine physical examinations, so eye, brain, CSF, and radiologic assessment are needed (Harrison 22e p.1802).
Toxoplasma pneumonia can be confused with Pneumocystis pneumonia, and organisms may also be found in healthy tissue, complicating interpretation (Harrison 22e p.1800).
If a patient is seronegative for T. gondii, the likelihood that a CNS mass lesion is due to toxoplasmosis is <10%, favoring earlier biopsy (Harrison 22e p.1802).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not provide a formal severity grading system for toxoplasmosis. Clinical stratification is by host immune status and syndrome: (1) immunocompetent acute infection - usually asymptomatic/self-limited (most commonly cervical lymphadenopathy); (2) ocular toxoplasmosis (chorioretinitis); (3) reactivation disease in the immunocompromised host - most importantly Toxoplasma encephalitis in AIDS (typically CD4+ <100/microL), which is rapidly fatal if untreated, plus pneumonitis, myocarditis, and disseminated disease; and (4) congenital toxoplasmosis, with severity inversely related to gestational age at maternal infection (earliest infection = lowest transmission but most severe fetal disease) (Harrison 22e p.1797-1800).
